title: The Price
corpus_scope: ICLR 2026 · 74,373 rated reviews of 19,467 papers · standards & stated rules: the nine-year corpus — 384 thousand reviewer pairs, 120,540 rule-stating reviews
question: What does each objection cost a paper in rating points, is that cost tied to whether the objection can be repaired, and does a stated rule price by what it says or by where it is aimed?

figures.title: The tariff: the price of each objection, paper held fixed
figures.deck: Holding the paper fixed, a novelty objection travels with well over twice the score deficit of any other charge.

claims.statement: A novelty objection costs −0.43 points on the 2026 rating scale, holding the paper and criticism volume fixed — 2.4 times the next charge.
claims.derivation: novelty's within-paper coefficient is −0.429; the next-largest negative-signed coefficient among objects whose 95% interval excludes zero is problem framing at −0.179; 0.429 ÷ 0.179 = 2.40×

claims.statement: Framing costs −0.18, related work and baselines about −0.15.
claims.derivation: within-paper regression coefficients for problem_framing, related_work, baselines_ablations

figures.title: Price against repairability
figures.deck: The expensive charge is hand-made against this paper; the cheap ones are prescriptions.

claims.statement: The bill collects in one corner: novelty, 64% against 82–92% for everything else.
claims.derivation: with_improvement / n for novelty (5,977 / 9,409 = 63.5%, ≈64%), against 82–92% for the other eleven objects, joined against Fig. 14a's tariff coefficient

figures.title: Same bench, different law
figures.deck: Same paper, same object — and still, one split in three among pairs holding different standards travels with the standards alone.

claims.statement: Reviewer pairs who argued from the same standard reach opposite stances 20.5% of the time; pairs who argued from different standards, 30.1% — half again as often, and the bracketed +9.7 points is the split added by the standards alone.
claims.derivation: same-standard pair disagreement rate = 1 − law.dominant.same.agree = 20.5%; different-standard = 1 − law.dominant.diff.agree = 30.1%; difference = +9.7 points

claims.statement: The two thinnest rows (reproducibility, related work) rest on under 1,500 same-standard pairs.
claims.derivation: law.by_object[o].same.n for reproducibility (776) and related_work (1,335), both under the plate's 1,500 read-loosely threshold

figures.title: One law, twelve courtrooms: the evidence rule's tariff by docket
figures.deck: Aimed at what the paper claims to be (framing), the same rule keeps a −0.30σ deficit even with the review's criticism volume held fixed; aimed at how it is written (clarity), it costs nothing.

claims.statement: The identical evidence rule keeps a −0.30σ deficit in the framing docket and one indistinguishable from zero in clarity; the framing–clarity gap is −0.29σ (95% CI −0.38 to −0.20).
claims.derivation: dockets.problem_framing and dockets.clarity, the evidence_imported entry's .adj field (mean within-paper score deficit in σ, volume-regressed out)

figures.title: Inside the novelty docket: the price of each of its rules
figures.deck: Novelty's own rules — about combining or extending existing work — cost the most (−0.44 to −0.46σ, volume-adjusted); the borrowed evidence rule costs well under half that (−0.19).

claims.statement: Novelty's own rules sit at −0.44σ and beyond; the borrowed evidence rule costs −0.19 — the ×2.4 marked on the chart.
claims.derivation: dockets.novelty entries' .adj field: combination −0.4362, increment −0.4558, against the borrowed claims ("evidence rule (imported)") entry at −0.1926

caveats.text: Nobody assigned the objections at random: a reviewer who is already unconvinced is the one who raises novelty, so the number measures which objection travels with a low score, not what raising it would do. Read every price here as association, never causation.
caveats.scope: all Fig. 14 tariff and rule-price numbers

caveats.text: Fig. 14d/14e's prices are expressed in standard deviations of that year's own rating scale, because ICLR changed scales four times over 2018–2026, so four scoring regimes can share one axis.

The choice of standard is not prior to the judgment — it is part of it: which law a reviewer reaches for already carries most of the verdict they are about to give. Stance and standard are extracted from the same few units, so consistency of a reviewer's writing can contribute to the gap.
